entries.title: Britain's worst peacetime rail disaster
entries.desc: The 1952 Harrow & Wealdstone crash killed 112 people here — still the UK's deadliest peacetime rail accident. A memorial plaque is at the station.

entries.title: The Weald Stone
entries.desc: The sarsen stone (same rock as Stonehenge) that named the whole district. Grade II listed, unmarked, embedded in the pavement outside Bombay Central (ex-Red Lion pub). Vanished in 1549, reappeared in 1834.

entries.title: The Moon on the Hill
entries.desc: Nearest Spoons — down Station Road towards Harrow centre. Named after Orwell's essay on the perfect fictional pub, 'The Moon Under Water'.

entries.title: Harrow Skate Park
entries.desc: One of the country's oldest surviving skate parks, inside Byron Recreation Ground — 1970s concrete by renowned designer Adrian Rolt, whose sister park the 'Rom' in Romford is Grade II listed. A pilgrimage site for the UK skate scene.
entries.address: Byron Recreation Ground, Christchurch Ave, Wealdstone, HA3 5BD

entries.title: Byron Recreation Ground
entries.desc: Edwardian park named for Lord Byron, who was schooled at Harrow. Formal beds near the entrance, a line of Lombardy poplars, and the borough's leisure centre and skate park alongside.
entries.address: Byron Recreation Ground, Christchurch Ave, HA3 5BD

entries.title: Wealdstone Cemetery
entries.desc: Small, quiet 1902 burial ground tucked behind Byron park (entered through it), with serpentine paths, scattered war graves and gravestones set in grass — a proper hidden pocket of calm.
entries.address: via Byron Recreation Ground, Stuart Road entrance

entries.title: Headstone Manor & Museum
entries.desc: Moated 14th-century manor house with a free local-history museum and a medieval great barn, west towards Headstone.

entries.title: Little Venice & Browning's Pool
entries.desc: The basin where Regent's Canal meets the Grand Union. Named (jokingly) by Byron or Browning depending who you believe; the pool honours Browning, who lived here 25 years.

entries.title: Puppet Theatre Barge
entries.desc: A 50-seat marionette theatre inside a converted 1930s Thames lighter, moored in Little Venice Oct–June. Repertoire runs from Brer Rabbit to Lorca.

entries.title: The Prince Alfred
entries.desc: Spectacular 1860s Victorian pub, famous for its original carved 'snob screens' dividing the bar into five snugs you crawl between through waist-high doors.

entries.title: Waterbus to London Zoo
entries.desc: Canal boats run from Little Venice around Regent's Park to the Zoo and Camden — arriving at Camden Market by water beats the Northern line.
entries.address: Little Venice waterbus stop, Blomfield Road

entries.title: Turing was born up the road
entries.desc: Alan Turing was born at 2 Warrington Crescent, now the Colonnade Hotel — blue plaque on the front.

entries.title: Rembrandt Gardens
entries.desc: Small waterside garden on the edge of Browning's Pool — the best bench in Little Venice for watching the narrowboats. Named for Amsterdam's 1975 700th anniversary.

entries.title: The 'Ladies' Tube station'
entries.desc: When Maida Vale opened on 6 June 1915, it was the first Underground station staffed entirely by women — so extraordinary at the time it made The Times.

entries.title: Paddington Recreation Ground
entries.desc: Big Victorian rec ground just past the station — Roger Bannister trained here before his four-minute mile. Café, tennis, proper running track.

entries.title: The Metropolitan Bar
entries.desc: Spoons directly above the platforms, in the 1913 Chiltern Court Restaurant — cavernous hall with railway-company coats of arms on the ceiling. Entrance sits between two tube exits.

entries.title: Where the Underground began
entries.desc: Baker Street opened in 1863 on the Metropolitan Railway, the world's first underground line — it still runs beneath the Spoons. H.G. Wells lived in Chiltern Court above the station and wrote The Shape of Things to Come there.

entries.title: 221B & the Holmes statue
entries.desc: The Sherlock Holmes Museum trades as 221B Baker Street; a 3m bronze Holmes stands outside the station exit.

entries.title: Regent's Park
entries.desc: Two minutes north — 395 acres, the rose gardens in Queen Mary's Gardens are the best free flower display in London (peak June), plus the Open Air Theatre in summer.
